summary.text: A 27-year-old obese, nulliparous woman had a history of prolonged irregular menstrual bleeding since menarche at age 12, with heavy bleeding lasting more than 15 days per cycle from age 15. She did not seek treatment, developed recurrent symptomatic anemia with multiple hospital admissions for blood transfusions over the past 7 years, defaulted on gynecological follow-up in 2020, and subsequently received irregular treatment with hematinic and tranexamic acid. She had been married since 2020 and had not conceived without contraception.

She presented with severe anemia secondary to menorrhagia, with worsening lethargy, shortness of breath, palpitations and a syncopal episode a few weeks earlier. She appeared pale, with blood pressure 132/76 mm Hg, pulse 86 beats per minute and body mass index 37 kg/m^(2). A transabdominal scan showed an enlarged uterus and a hyperechoic intrauterine mass of 6.4 cm×3.0 cm with endometrial thickness 20 mm. Hemoglobin was 6.0 g/dL and blood was transfused.

The Pap smear was negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. Histopathology of endometrial tissue at hysteroscopy was consistent with endometrial endometrioid carcinoma (type 1), while the pipelle result is reported as a well-differentiated adenocarcinoma in the text but as atypical endometrial hyperplasia in the Figure 2 caption. CT showed an enlarged uterus with a 6.4 cm×3.2 cm intrauterine mass, with no signs of liver or lung metastases, and MRI did not reveal endometrial invasion.

Because she expressed concerns about conception, management focused on medical therapies for fertility preservation: a hormonal intrauterine device was inserted and high-dose oral progesterone was administered. Regular follow-ups were planned to monitor disease progression and prepare for future pregnancies.

article_limitations: The Figure 2 caption (atypical endometrial hyperplasia) conflicts with the case text citing Figure 2 for the pipelle result (well-differentiated endometrioid adenocarcinoma, FIGO grade 1); both are kept as review-only observations and the FIGO grade is not recorded as an include fact.

The discussion sentence that the prolonged interval from symptom onset to cancer may be explained by missed follow-up, the sentence that delays in seeking care resulted in serious outcomes, and the risk statement about obesity are author interpretations or non-specific and are not recorded as separate clinical facts.
Hyperplasia is recorded only as a possible, unconfirmed condition from a discussion sentence.

The discussion sentence that the patient was treated with an LNGIUS and high-dose progesterone refers to this patient (no citation in the sentence) and is recorded in oncology.treatments without a tumor link as its own timeline event; it is not literally identified with the hormonal intrauterine device in the case text, so the two are not merged.
No sex is recorded for the husband (the source prints "His husband"); no supplements and no tables exist; three single-panel figures were viewed in visual.json.
Written informed consent (b00010) is administrative and is not recorded as a fact.
